title: Breaking and Entering: Melbourne's Gym For Synths MESS Celebrates 10 Years
summary: MESS (Melbourne Electronic Sound Studio) celebrates its 10th anniversary this year! Co-founders Byron Scullin and Robin Fox join Lauren in the studio to reflect on the creation of their "living museum". Located in Federation Square, MESS houses a significant collection of new and historic electronic instruments and preserves them for use by musicians from all over the world.
transcript:
Byron Scullin and Robin Fox, co-founders of Melbourne Electronic Sound Studio (MESS), joined Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studios to mark its 10th anniversary. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 7 May 2026.

Lauren: Lovely to have you both here, looking back at 10 years of MESS today.

Guest: It's great to be here. Thanks, Lauren.

Lauren: Has this anniversary, looking back at 10 years, been a reflective time for you both?

Robin: Yes. Yeah, it really has. It's been an epic, epic journey. I mean, I guess it's been more than 10 years too, because we started hatching the idea quite a bit of time before we opened the doors. And I sometimes describe MESS as a beautiful migraine, and it feels like one that we've had for 10 years now. But it's extraordinary. We've just opened in Federation Square: huge change last year, huge, huge bit of growth. But I don't know, how old are you feeling?

Byron: I don't know. The thing about MESS is that some days you go in there, after 10 years of all this work, and just with Robin and I starting with the initial idea, and initially doing everything ourselves, and working at it every day, and now it's kind of its own thing. It has its own staff, and it runs itself, really, in a lot of ways. So it can feel quite rejuvenating, actually, to be in there still, and to see this continual growth, and new people looking in through the windows at Federation Square and discovering what MESS actually is. It's kind of the energy that people bring to it, actually, that makes it always continually exciting, even though at times it can be a bit like, “Oh no, not another PDF to fill out,” or, “Not another email to send.”

Lauren: For people who don't know MESS, we are talking about Melbourne Electronic Sound Studio. The theme of your decade of MESS celebrations is past, present and future, and you've said, just like feedback in an audio circuit, that you're treating those concepts as interrelated. I want to ask you both if we can look back to the past a bit, the origin story, and to tell us maybe how you both connected, and why you decided to start MESS.

Byron: Well, I guess Robin and I knew each other through the kind of experimental music scene here in Melbourne, and we'd both kind of come from some different backgrounds, I guess, in that regard. And I think at the point in time when the MESS conversation arose, we were really a bit frustrated with what the opportunities were that existed, both in terms of people wanting to have access to these old machines, and a shared fascination that we had with this electronic music-making equipment. And then from one point of view, thinking that institutions like educational institutions or museums were supposed to be the benefactors of this stuff, but having both worked in those institutions, seeing that it really wasn't there. But then also, I guess, just the excitement of being able to use these things and have access to them.

And I guess in some ways too, even just how we'd come to know each other through, I don't know, hanging out at gigs and hanging out at record stores, and just seeing the way that people were able to connect with each other over music. And thinking that between all these various frustrations and perceived opportunities, there might be something there, an idea that we could develop out of those ideas.

Robin: Yeah, and I guess dropping into all of that energy was the fact that I was incredibly fortunate to inherit Keith Humble's electronic music studio, which is really a big part of why we could be having these conversations. Because I had these instruments that were becoming increasingly valuable, increasingly rare, and very difficult for people to find. And for me personally, I was on tour quite a bit back then, and I wasn't going to be using them as much as I thought I should be. And so we had this notion that maybe there would be a way to make that a bit more open.

But it was when we started talking to our mutual friend Wally de Backer, aka Gotye, who had, when he had his extraordinary success with his single, bought a lot of electronic musical instruments that he'd been fascinated with over time. And he's generous to a fault, Wally, and an amazing human being. And when we talked about this idea, he kind of said, “Well, I've got this big collection of instruments. You could have access to those, and merge them with the Keith Humble collection, and kind of make them available to people to play.” And one thing led to another, and before long, on paper, we had this extraordinary collection of instruments that we could weaponise, if you like, for public good. And that really gave us the impetus, and the cachet, to open the doors. And we opened the doors on April Fool's in 2016, from memory, not as a joke, but it just happened to be the time that it was ready.

And I know there were moments where we never thought we'd be ready. We had no models to go on. I mean, we're a charitable organisation. We're not trying to make any money, but we also had to insure and care for a multi-million-dollar collection of instruments. And so it was a really interesting proposition and an experiment, basically. It's a great social experiment. And what's been beautiful is just to watch the community that's grown around it: the community of artists, the community of enthusiasts, and just a lot of passionate people and a lot of very generous people. We've managed to get together a really beautiful family of patrons who help us. And the government helps us through Creative Australia and Creative Victoria, and the City of Melbourne do their part. [Unclear audio at 00:05:47–00:05:52] Such an amazing place. Really, really does do wonderful things for the city.

So it's a tapestry of things that we have to put together to make it all work. But it's as Byron said: now that we're in Federation Square, we literally went from zero foot traffic in the bunker in North Melbourne to about 400,000 a year or something. So now people who didn't know they were interested in electronic music, they now are interested in it. But we're also about much more than the instruments. The instruments are really just the honeypot for us to get people into the space and get creative. And we're big believers in the fact that a creative life is a happy one. And so many people seem cut off from the creative process now that it's amazing to me how many people will come into MESS and say, “I can't make music.” And you go, “Well, you're human, so you actually can. You've just got to allow yourself to do it.” And so giving people permission to unlock that side of their lives is really what we're about, and just making the world a better place. And we're doing that one step at a time, hopefully.

Lauren: You said when you started MESS that you were very conscious of what could happen: that it could become this bro den of dudes patching synths and talking shop. And you were telling us, I think when Simon and I came to see you guys down in the bunker, back in, I think it was like 2019, in North Melbourne, that when you started MESS, you put the call out first to women and trans and non-binary people to join. Are you finding there's been a shift in popularity in those particular workshops that you've been doing, 10 years on, compared to when you first started MESS?

Byron: I think they've — I mean, they've always been well attended. And I think it was just us trying to make sure that we had as many different kinds of people in the studio making music as possible, because it just meant that there was more different kinds of music then being made, and out in the world, and being heard by people. And so I guess in that regard, those areas have always been really thriving. And I think that also people from those various communities too were looking for an opportunity to be able to congregate together, and to come and be with each other, and enjoy electronic music in a way that was with their own people.

So in many ways, Robin and I kind of definitely consulted and talked with people about that stuff, and then kind of got out of the way and just let those people use the space. And made sure that people at MESS as well were kind of representative of various groups, so that anybody who walks into MESS at any time can see people that they feel familiar with, and see people who they might know, or who they might feel comfortable with, and then just allow things to happen from there. So it's not too forced, I guess, in that regard. And authentic community can't really be made. It's just allowing for the conditions for it to take place, I think, was the really important thing that we focused on early. And then as other people have come in and contributed in different ways to the organisation, that's just grown and grown.

Robin: And part of creating that context is recognising that these spaces have traditionally been male-dominated, and been incredibly intimidating for non-male people, basically. And so just being very conscious of that, and being conscious of the fact that we didn't want to perpetuate that, was very important to us.

Byron: Yeah, and just listening to folks too. As MESS has gone on, I think it's improved mostly because of people contributing and feeding back into that process. So as much as Robin and I had the seed of this initial idea, the thing that brings the richness and the growth to MESS is, as Robin had mentioned earlier, all the contributions from various people, whether that's our supporters and patrons, and even just people that walk through the door every day. Just being there, and being present in the space, is enough to contribute.

Robin: And our members, of course.

Byron: Of course. It's unbelievable. And as you know, as a membership organisation here at Triple R, being a member is a form of patronage that's really important in the cultural sector at the moment.

Lauren: So is it correct that you were inspired by radio stations like Triple R with the…?

Byron: Oh yeah, absolutely. Triple R, and I guess both our interactions with Triple R, and just seeing, because Triple R has been this amazing organisation in Melbourne, and world-renowned because of the fact that it has remained this independent media entity over such a long period of time, and intergenerationally now, it's been around for so long. So I guess when Robin and I were first looking at the model, Triple R came up quite a lot, in terms of: here was this amazing organisation that's been able to sustain itself, where a lot of people felt welcome, that had a really diverse range of voices represented on it and around it, and a diverse range of activity that occurred around it as well. And so for us it was actually a gold standard in many ways.

And MESS can be a hard thing to describe to people too, because it's a new type of organisation. It's a living museum, it's a bit of an education institution, it's an arts organisation, and all these various things. But basically, it's a gym for synths. That's the best way to describe it, because then people know they get a membership and come and use it. But Triple R was, I guess, a real landmark for us in terms of developing the idea. And I think it's also a real landmark in terms of what makes Melbourne such an amazing place: these various independent organisations that all kind of are in dialogue with each other. And it just leads to, I guess, the cultural richness of a place like Melbourne, and what makes it great for people who live here, but also what draws people to Melbourne.

Lauren: Totally. Your collection of synths and rare instruments runs really, really deep. I believe there's pieces in there from the 1920s to today as well. You've got a lot of international visitors and creatives from around the world who come and visit MESS: Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, who we just played, and Suzanne Ciani, who played earlier in the show as well. Is there a particular synth in the collection that's most impressive to those visitors?

Robin: It's funny, because a lot of the international artists that come through have amazing collections of synths. So I guess one story I could tell in that regard is that Alessandro Cortini came through the studio once. Really lovely guy. Some people know him from his role in Nine Inch Nails, but he also has an incredible practice as an electronic musician himself, and a phenomenal collection of instruments. And he's particularly drawn to early Buchla synthesisers. So when he came in, he kind of looked around, and for him, he's got most of the stuff that's in the studio, so he's pretty difficult to impress. But we do have certain things in the collection that are literally unicorn machines. And one of them is called the VCS1, which came from the Keith Humble collection.

And it was commissioned by an Australian composer called Don Banks, who famously threw down 50 pounds in a British pub, and he threw that money at Tristram Cary, Peter Zinovieff and David Cockerell, all the three people who then went on to found the EMS synthesiser company, which made some of the most iconic synthesisers of today. Just look it up, it's amazing. Pink Floyd, [name uncertain: “brown”], all those people back in the — he did this in the very late 60s, early 70s. He actually asked them for a synth he could take to bed and patch in bed, and so they made him this portable, patchable synthesiser. And then Keith Humble got interested and ordered one, and then there was one other one. So there's only three of these instruments that were ever made, and they were actually the precursor to one of the most famous synthesiser companies that emerged in the 1970s. So it's a real piece of history.

And so I guess when I pointed that out to Alessandro, he kind of went a little bit quiet and said, “I want to play that one,” and then went on to kind of explore that synthesiser. So even for the aficionados, you'll be able to find something in the collection that is truly unique. And it's also not just the uniqueness of the instruments, but the fact that you can walk in off the street and play a theremin that was hand-built by Theremin in New York in the late — early 1930s, the one that we have. The fact that you can just come in and play that is the most extraordinary thing, because you might find something like that in a museum, but no one's ever going to let you turn it on and listen to it. And as far as we're concerned, these things are musical instruments. They should be heard. And I think that a lot of the people who support our organisation really support that feeling as well. You don't lock musical instruments up behind glass and look at them. You play them. That's what they're for.

Lauren: And playing helps to preserve them as well, doesn't it?

Guest: Yeah, it does, particularly in relation to older analogue machines. None of these instruments too, it should be said, are inherently iconic. They become iconic because of what people make with them, and what they do with them. And so I think in many ways with MESS, we hope that there are just future icons sitting there, and that some artist is going to come in and make something, and that's going to fire up people's imaginations, or create a beautiful piece of music that everyone can share in, and then a new icon arrives. But that can't happen if they're sitting in a compactus, or if they're sitting behind Perspex or behind glass. So this model, I guess, of, as you say, preservation through use, is very important to us.

Byron: Because if these machines are sitting in a museum dungeon somewhere, not being used because they're too important to use, it's kind of like, and this might be a bit strong, but it's a form of vandalisation, because they're just degrading through not being used. And also you're not giving people the opportunity to use their potential. And they're not that old. As Robin said, some of the real golden age of electronic music begins in the late 1960s. So whilst in terms of musical fashion we sometimes think that they might be old, in terms of history they're very recent. And it's a little strange to think: well, what other musical instrument would you suddenly lock in a compactus after 20 years because it was too important to use? It's a little bit absurd in some ways as well.

Lauren: I saw Jarvis Cocker was visiting recently. What particular synth was he taken by when he dropped into MESS?

Guest: He was such a sweet guy, by the way. So for any fans of Jarvis out there, he's not one of those people who, when you meet your heroes, they turn out to be monsters. He wasn't at all. Super sweet guy. And he came in, he was drawn first of all to the Novachord. And again, this is an extraordinary instrument that we have in the collection. It's from the 1930s. It's a very early Hammond, and it was the first ever commercially available polyphonic synthesiser, the first time you could play more than one note at a time on an electronic synthesiser that you could buy. It has 163 valves in it. It weighs a couple of tons. So he kind of looked at it and said, “What the hell is that?” And then sat down and played the Novachord for a little while.

And then he was drawn to another instrument, the Roland System 100, which is a beautiful set. We've got the complete set. It's immaculate, looks really amazing. And he was making some interesting sounds with it. I was listening to him play through the speakers, and he was just finding his way with the instrument, so I wandered over and said, “Would you like to record some of this?” And he just said, “I am.” And he had his phone sitting in the middle of the two speakers, so obviously a hi-fi aficionado. But he dropped a reference to MESS in his concert at the Bowl, which was really lovely, and made the joke that he'd recorded his next album there. So let's see. Let's see what happens.

Byron: It's funny too, because actually the way that that System 100 came to us was another crazy story, where the MESS studio manager at the time, Matt Watson, came into the studio one morning, and there was a message on the answering machine. And he played it back, and it was the Australian actor Guy Pearce, who'd left a message and said, “I've got a couple of synthesisers, maybe you'd be interested in having them as part of your collection.” And so Matt called Guy back and got it sorted out. So the System 100 is owned by Guy Pearce, and is loaned to us as part of the MESS collection. And we've not yet met Guy. He hasn't come down to the studio, but we have this couple of instruments there that belong to him. And I guess that's part of the thing: it's kind of constantly surprising to Rob and I that MESS's reputation has gone far and wide, and that people will quite often give us a call on the phone and say, “I've got this synth that's sitting around, and maybe you guys are interested in making sure it's available for people.”

Guest: I think it's amazing that people kind of see the attraction of having this amazing thing, and then going, “Well, I'm not really using it, but I can lend it to this organisation, and then they can let people have the joy of using it.” I like to think of MESS as quite an act of generosity, basically, because we are just doing this so that people can come and use these things. And I think that that act of generosity is a bit contagious. So when Guy was wondering what to do with these synthesisers, he wanted to do something generous with it, and we can facilitate that. So we can be a funnel for people's generosity.

Lauren: Incredible. Have you got some fun stuff planned in the works for the year?

Byron: We're just trying to work out which synth is going to be the cake. We're arguing about that.

Robin: Yeah, exactly. Which one are we going to kind of carve up and consume in a new way? Look, there are some things in the wind, but nothing I can talk about at the moment. But basically the whole program is being bound up in this idea of past, present and future. We're thinking about that theme a lot. And so we recently had the 13th iteration of our Sonorous commissions, which are our octophonic commissions. And at each one of those, we play a work from the Australian electronic music archive. So the idea of Sonorous really encapsulates this idea that we commission artists to engage with a collection from the past, to make something in the present that will affect people in the future. So it is this kind of feedback proposition. And including that little archival work is also just there to drop that in there, because the whole idea of the past, present, future came from the idea that we do hold a really historically significant collection.

And we tell a lot of really interesting stories, particularly Australian stories from the history of electronic music, that a lot of people don't know. And it is always great to know your own local history. It can empower you in the sense moving forward. And so that's the point: to empower people in the present to then make work that will live into the future.

And somebody did blow my mind recently. This is something that a lot of people know already, but I felt it for the first time the other day: that the past, of course, is completely intangible, and the future is completely intangible. So all of them exist literally just in your mind, in the present. That idea of the eternal present just suddenly landed for me the other day, and I found it quite mind-blowing. So there's kind of no such thing as either of those things. It's just what we have now. There's nostalgia and there's anxiety. Nostalgia is the past, anxiety is the future. But the present is what's important, and presence is what's important. So we're all about bringing people together.

Byron: And I think along with that, one thing that we are doing this year is these public tours, free public tours that people can come and join along with. Because we're in Federation Square, we're just trying to find more and more ways to open up the collection for people to come and use. And those public tours are really great, because people can come down, hear some of these stories that Robin mentions, but also hear the machines make some of these sounds. And it's funny how making some sounds from the past, and having the machine in front of you actually doing it, really kind of, I think, underscores that thing that Robin's saying, of like, it's ever present. And I think people get a real kick out of hearing these machines make these sounds that maybe they have really deep memories of and connections to, through their own musical listening experiences that they've had, and their own associations that they bring of listening to music in times and places, and how much emotion that can [Unclear audio at 00:22:20–00:22:21].

I mean, we've got an amazing instrument in there, the Fairlight CMI, which is this Australian icon. And I remember doing a talk a few years ago down in Warrnambool, and just playing a whole selection of 80s: Kate Bush, and so many Trevor Horn productions, and Afrika Bambaataa, and Herbie Hancock, and the list goes on and on. Stevie Wonder. But suddenly I was playing little snippets of all these tracks, and there was a woman in the audience who was [Unclear audio at 00:22:49–00:22:50] to tears. She's like, “Oh my God, it's overwhelming, all the nostalgia and these memories, and so much association in my life of all these amazing moments.” And just hearing these sounds, and hearing this story about this iconic Australian instrument that's really changed the face of electronic music, it was just a whirlwind of emotion for her. And I think a lot of people connect in various ways to that thing. It's this great thing to see it all come together in a place like MESS.

Lauren: We should of course mention, before we wind up, that I announced yesterday there is a campaign, MESS for All, a matching campaign where every dollar you give to MESS is doubled until May 31st as well.

Guest: So this is a really great opportunity. I mean, people often, I find, don't think of themselves as philanthropists. But like I said before, I consider MESS members philanthropists. If you become a member of MESS, I consider you a donor to our cause. But as a charitable organisation, we're not trying to make money. And what we're about is removing barriers to entry to the creative process. And one of the programs that Creative Australia runs is called the Plus1 funding program. And so we were successful in securing a $50,000 pledge from the government, as long as we could raise that $50,000 by May 31st. So the MESS for All campaign actually has a joke that'll roll out later, a MESS for All and All for MESS, like a Three Musketeers kind of thing.

And so the idea is to try and encourage people to donate to the organisation at this critical time, because every dollar you donate will be matched by the government, up to $50,000. So you can double the impact of your donation. And the donations are going directly towards the establishment of a more formal pathways program that we really want to pioneer, this suite of programs that will reduce those barriers to entry, across free places in our courses, but also dedicated workshops for marginalised communities. So it's a really great cause. I mean, it's often a difficult sell when you've got a huge collection of synthesisers. People seem to think you're rich. We're not rich. It's a charitable organisation. The people own these machines. We don't own the machines.

And it's also, I guess, a really abstract notion, because we're not curing cancer, but I like to say that we're preventing it, by creating happiness and wellness for people through access to the creative process. So that's a grandiose claim. But it is a really great cause, and the clock's ticking on that one. So I don't think anyone's got any spare cash at the moment, but if you do, please consider MESS as a place for it.

Lauren: Get involved, and keep an eye on the MESS website for upcoming plans for the 10th anniversary celebrations. Congratulations for all you've achieved in the last 10 years with MESS, and good luck for all going forward as well. Robin Fox and Byron Scullin from Melbourne Electronic Sound Studio, thank you very much for joining me on Breaking and Entering today.

Guest: Absolute pleasure. Thanks, Lauren.
